COP31 organisers have characterised this year's summit as a “COP of implementation”, focused on making commitments happen as opposed to making sweeping new statements. Simon Stiell, the head of UN Climate Change, addressed the plenary session of COP31, saying, "Progress is not nearly enough or fair enough."

There are three main tracks: emissions, where countries will make good on their stronger Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement; finance, which involves fulfilling the new collective quantified finance goal agreed to at COP29; and adaptation and resilience for vulnerable countries. The financing track is expected to be the most difficult, with developing countries demanding faster access to finance.

The Presidency’s Action Agenda includes a global electrification goal of “35 by 2035.” The International Energy Agency estimates that electricity could provide 33 percent of the world’s final energy consumption by 2035 (just shy of the goal), up from 23 percent today.

Monday was Food, Agriculture and Health Day, focusing on climate effects on human health against the backdrop of an impending El Niño with extreme weather effects. Negotiators will also discuss fossil fuels language, which producers such as Saudi Arabia and Russia will oppose once again.

The United States is not sending a delegation, continuing the Trump administration's withdrawal from climate diplomacy. Some Democratic lawmakers, including Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, are attending independently.

headline: Amazon unveils $250 AI-powered drone camera that flies around your house to catch intruders
subheadline: Drone cam uses its AI Pilot technology to map indoor spaces, avoid obstacles and follow predetermined flight routes
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Amazon has unveiled an AI-powered security camera with capabilities to fly across rooms, investigate suspicious activity and patrol homes without anyone controlling its movements.

The Ring Drone Cam, priced at $249.99, was unveiled on Tuesday. It is designed to take off automatically whenever a connected security sensor detects unusual activity, allowing homeowners to keep watch at their house when they are away.

It isn’t like a traditional CCTV camera that remains fixed at one location instead it is a flying device that can navigate around furniture, check different rooms and stream live footage directly to a smartphone.

Users can schedule regular patrols and even send the drone cam to investigate a particular area through the Ring App.

The flying camera offers a 2k resolution and comes equipped with built-in lights to capture footage in dark rooms.

Amazon says the drone uses its AI Pilot technology to map indoor spaces, avoid obstacles and follow predetermined flight routes.

When not operating, it returns to a charging dock, where its camera automatically switches off.

However, the device has limitations, including a flight time of approximately five to eight minutes before it needs recharging.

The company has also introduced a $999.99 Ring Rover Cam, a wheeled security robot designed to patrol businesses, investigate disturbances and record video in up to 4K resolution.

Both devices are part of Ring Robotics, Amazon's latest push into autonomous home and business security.

The flying camera is scheduled to begin shipping in the United States on January 27, 2027, nearly seven years after Amazon first demonstrated a similar concept in 2020.

However, it still requires authorisation from the US Federal Communications Commission before it can be sold.

headline: Kris Jenner, 71, celebrates boyfriend Corey Gamble on his 46th birthday
subheadline: Kris Jenner began dating Corey Gamble in 2014 when she was finalising her divorce from Caitlyn Jenner
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Kris Jenner is celebrating her boyfriend Corey Gamble’s special day.

As Gamble turned 46 years old on Tuesday, November 10, the Kardashian-Jenner matriarch - who celebrated her 71st birthday on Thursday — took to Instagram with a sweet birthday tribute.

“Happy birthday to my love, @coreygamble,” Jenner wrote alongside a carousel of images with her partner-of-16-years. “I feel so lucky to do life with you.”

READ MORE: Corey Gamble calls Kris Jenner 'lil wife' in 71st birthday tribute

The momager went on to thank Gamble for his dedication to her and her six children, including Kourtney, Kim, Khloe, and Rob Kardashian, as well as Kendall and Kylie Jenner.

“Thank you for all you do for me and for all of us, every single day. Thank you for always being there for us, for the love you give, for the laughter and joy you bring, and for making even the most ordinary moments feel special. I love you babe,” she wrote.

Just days earlier on November 5, Gamble penned a heartfelt birthday wish for Jenner, calling her his “lil wife” and “the greatest mother.”

The pair have been dating since 2014, but they haven’t tied the knot. Jenner previously explained her decision to not get married, telling Laura Wasser on the Divorce Sucks podcast in 2018 that she’s “already had the big wedding” and “the babies and the kids” with ex-husbands Rob Kardashian and Caitlyn Jenner.

“I’m in a really great relationship right now, and I’m happy and I don’t want to mess that up,” she admitted.

headline: Prince Harry joins forces with European Parliament for new memorial
subheadline: Prince Harry backs major push to protect children online with poignant Brussels appearance
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Prince Harry has joined European leaders and campaigners in Brussels to call for stronger protections for children online, as a powerful new memorial honouring young victims of online violence was unveiled at the European Parliament.

The Duke of Sussex attended the launch of the Lost Screen Memorial, an initiative organised by Archewell Philanthropies in partnership with the European Parliament Intergroup on Children’s Rights.

The memorial brings together the stories of families whose children died after experiencing online violence, highlighting the devastating consequences of abuse and harmful behaviour on digital platforms.

Read More: Prince Harry mobbed by locals in mother Diana's home county

Rather than focusing on statistics, the installation gives a voice to the families left behind, sharing their experiences and the pain they continue to endure.

It also raises questions about the role of technology companies, platform design and the safeguards in place to protect young and vulnerable users.

Harry was among the speakers at the unveiling, alongside European Parliament President Roberta Metsola and MEP López-Istúriz, the first vice-chair of the Children’s Rights Intergroup.

Following the ceremony, López-Istúriz praised Harry and Archewell for helping bring the issue before European lawmakers and supporting efforts to turn calls for change into action.

He called for tougher legislation across the EU, better prevention measures, greater support for victims and their families, and a global coalition capable of holding technology companies accountable.

“These families deserve more than sympathy. They deserve action,” he said, stressing that children’s safety must not be negotiable.

headline: Can Pete Hegseth be removed from office? US impeachment process explained
subheadline: Democrats are set to take control of Congress in January
author: Web Desk
article_text:
US War Secretary Pete Hegseth is facing an impeachment threat after a Republican lawmaker introduced eight charges against him, raising questions about how Congress could remove President Donald Trump's Pentagon chief from office.

Republican Congressman Thomas Massie filed the resolution on Monday, accusing Hegseth of abusing his powers, particularly by conducting military operations against Iran without congressional authorisation.

The charges also concern US military operations in Yemen, Venezuela and the Caribbean.

Hegseth has rejected the allegations, calling the impeachment effort a "political spectacle", while Trump has pledged to stand by him.

How does the US impeachment process work?

Step 1: Introducing impeachment charges

A member of the House of Representatives introduces articles of impeachment outlining alleged misconduct. The Constitution allows impeachment for treason, bribery or other "high crimes and misdemeanors".

Step 2: House considers the charges

House leaders can seek to dismiss the resolution, refer it to a committee for investigation or allow lawmakers to debate the allegations.

In Hegseth's case, Republican leaders could attempt to block Massie's resolution through a procedural vote.

Step 3: Voting on impeachment

If the charges reach a House vote, a simple majority is required to impeach Hegseth.

US War Secretary Pete Hegseth is facing an impeachment threat after a Republican lawmaker introduced eight charges against him, raising questions about how Congress could remove President Donald Trump's Pentagon chief from office.

Republican Congressman Thomas Massie filed the resolution on Monday, accusing Hegseth of abusing his powers, particularly by conducting military operations against Iran without congressional authorisation.

The charges also concern US military operations in Yemen, Venezuela and the Caribbean.

Hegseth has rejected the allegations, calling the impeachment effort a "political spectacle", while Trump has pledged to stand by him.

How does the US impeachment process work?

Step 1: Introducing impeachment charges

A member of the House of Representatives introduces articles of impeachment outlining alleged misconduct. The Constitution allows impeachment for treason, bribery or other "high crimes and misdemeanors".

Step 2: House considers the charges

House leaders can seek to dismiss the resolution, refer it to a committee for investigation or allow lawmakers to debate the allegations.

In Hegseth's case, Republican leaders could attempt to block Massie's resolution through a procedural vote.

If the charges reach a House vote, a simple majority is required to impeach Hegseth.

Conviction requires a two-thirds majority of senators present. If convicted, Hegseth would immediately lose his position. The Senate could also vote separately to bar him from holding future federal office.

If acquitted, he would remain in office.

The Republican-controlled House has yet to confirm a final impeachment vote outcome, while Democrats are set to take control of Congress in January following their midterm election victories.

Massie's resolution could expire when the current Congress ends on January 3, 2027, unless lawmakers act on it before then.

headline: Within 50 kilometers: The 520 million children living near war
subheadline: Thirty years after the world promised to protect them, more children live near conflict than at any point on record
author: Quratulain Akram
article_text:
Last December, UNICEF’s Catherine Russell met a girl in Sudan named Nahed. She was 16 when war broke out. Her family fled Khartoum, Sudan for a village they believed was safe, but the war followed them. Armed men attacked, killing her grandfather and uncle. Girls were raped and abducted. Nahed escaped, though what she witnessed didn’t leave her.

Russell told the UN Security Council that behind every violation is a child whose life may never be the same. The sentence is worth holding onto, because everything that follows is arithmetic, and arithmetic has a way of making suffering feel tidy.

The numbers, however, are not today. The Peace Research Institute Oslo, in an analysis commissioned by Save the Children, estimates that 520 million children, 20.7% of the world’s children, lived in a conflict zone in 2024. That is the highest figure ever recorded. In the mid-1990s the share was about one in ten.

The method deserves precision. A child counts as affected if she/he lives within 50 kilometers of a lethal conflict event. A radius chosen because that violence at that distance disrupts daily life through insecurity, displacement, and lost services. It is a measure of exposure, not of injury. Even so, it describes a planet where it had become an ambient condition of childhood. Africa has now both the largest number of affected children (218 million) and the highest share (32.6%).

The UN’s own tally is narrower and grimmer. It has verified more than 430,000 grave violations against children since 2005, more than 38,000 of them in 2025, the highest annual figure since the Council took the issue.

The worst-affected places were the State of Palestine, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Nigeria. It is important to note that these are the only cases the UN could verify. In war, the verifiable is a floor, not a ceiling.

The pattern of harm is telling. More than 70% of verified child casualties in 2025 came from explosive weapons, which also destroyed the schools, hospitals, and water systems that sustain children afterward. The UN recorded more than 8,000 incidents of denied humanitarian access that year. Government forces, not only insurgents, were responsible for the majority of verified violations.

Not all damage arrives with a blast. The American Academy of Pediatrics, in a March 2026 policy statement, notes that the UN estimated more than 52 million children were out of school because of conflict in 2024. Girls in conflict zones are about 2.5 times more likely than boys to be out of school, and less likely to return. School closure, the statement warns, raises the risk of exploitation, early marriage, and recruitment.

This is where the story turns from the visible to the invisible. A child out of school is not a casualty in any dataset of violations, yet she has lost one of the strongest protections she had. Her loss is also a society’s loss.

Since Graca Machel’s 1996 report, which found that 2 million children had been killed in conflict in the preceding decade, the world has built monitoring mechanisms, signed more than 40 action plans with parties to conflict, and secured the release of more than 220,000 children from armed forces and groups.

And still the trajectory worsens. Here the diagnosis splits. Russell argues for sustained political will, protected funding and real diplomacy, noting that aid can’t substitute for ending wars. Waltz counters that after 30 years, success can’t be measured by reports produced or meetings held, and that existing resources must be judged by outcomes.

Both are right about something. Verification is not protection, and a system that documents violations ever more precisely while they multiply is measuring its own failure. But results require the shelters, counselor, and monitors that budget cuts are now dismantling as childhood doesn’t pause for diplomacy, and no mechanism, however well-designed, can give back the years.

Both are right about something. Verification is not protection, and a system that documents violations ever more precisely while they multiply is measuring its own failure. But results require the shelters, counselor, and monitors that budget cuts are now dismantling as childhood doesn’t pause for diplomacy, and no mechanism, however well-designed, can give back the years.

headline: Ch Salik says he did not name CM Maryam in corruption remarks, response to notice ready
subheadline: Minister says after controversy, Punjab govt withdrew Elite Force security provided to him for 18 months
author: Raees Ansari
article_text:
Says Shafay was unaware of his remarks and can decide on resignation.
Says reply to Maryam's notice ready, to be made public in days.
Maryam seeks Rs5bn in damages over corruption remarks.

LAHORE: Federal Minister for Overseas Pakistanis Chaudhry Salik Hussain has said he did not mention Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz by name in his recent remarks about alleged corruption in the province, as he revealed that the Punjab government had withdrawn his Elite Force security.

Speaking to reporters in Lahore, Salik sought to clarify his remarks amid a growing dispute with Maryam, who subsequently served him a Rs5 billion defamation notice.

"I did not mention Maryam Nawaz by name," he said.

The federal minister also confirmed that the Punjab government had withdrawn his security, adding that Elite Force personnel had been accompanying him for around one-and-a-half years.

Asked whether his elder brother, Punjab Minister for Industries, Commerce and Investment Chaudhry Shafay Hussain, would resign from the provincial cabinet following the controversy, Salik said his brother had not known about his remarks beforehand.

"He did not know that I was going to make the statement. Only he can answer the question about his resignation," Salik said.

He added that he had prepared his response to the legal notice and would make it public within a few days.

The controversy

The latest development follows a public dispute that erupted after Salik criticised the Punjab government's governance and alleged widespread corruption in the province during an interview with a private television channel.

The Pakistan Muslim League-Quaid (PML-Q) leader had praised his paternal uncle, former Punjab chief minister Chaudhry Pervez Elahi, describing him as the best chief executive Punjab had ever had.

He also alleged that political considerations were influencing development priorities and the allocation of public funds, claiming that a disproportionate share of Punjab's development budget was being channelled towards Lahore while other districts were being overlooked.

Salik said he regularly heard accounts of corruption in the province, adding that there were so many alleged corruption-related files that they could fill entire cupboards.

He acknowledged that he did not possess documentary evidence to substantiate the claims but maintained that corruption was taking place.

Maryam subsequently announced legal action against the federal minister, challenging him to produce evidence or face proceedings. She also questioned why he continued to serve in a government he considered corrupt.

The chief minister linked the controversy to the appointment of the deputy commissioner in Gujrat, alleging that Salik was unhappy because an officer of his choice had not been appointed.

Salik, however, rejected the suggestion that his remarks were prompted by the appointment, saying the interview had been recorded weeks earlier.

Maryam later served a Rs5 billion defamation notice on Salik, as well as a news anchor and a television channel's chairman, demanding a retraction, an unconditional apology and damages over the remarks.

The notice accused them of making and broadcasting sweeping, unsubstantiated allegations that had damaged the reputation of the chief minister and the provincial administration.

Salik has maintained his position on the corruption issue and said he would respond through the appropriate legal process.

The controversy has also drawn attention to the position of his brother Shafay, who serves in Maryam's provincial cabinet.

Shafay had earlier said he stood by his younger brother and would not distance himself from him, adding that Salik had his own independent views.

The two brothers belong to the PML-Q, led by their father Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain, whose family's political alignments have diverged in recent years.

While Chaudhry Pervez Elahi and his son Moonis Elahi aligned themselves with the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), Shujaat Hussain's sons Salik and Shafay have remained aligned with the Sharif-led political camp.

headline: Brenda Song gives parenting advice to her 'Suite Life' costar Dylan Sprouse
subheadline: Dylan Sprouse recently welcomed his first child with his wife, Barbara Palvin
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Dylan Sprouse is deep in the trenches of new parenthood with his wife Barbara Palvin, and his Suite Life of Zack & Cody costar Brenda Song knows the struggles all too well.

Naturally, the actress — who shares two kids with her fiancé Macaulay Culkin — had to give some crucial parenting advice to Sprouse when she appeared on the latest episode of his Wildman podcast on November 10.

“The craziest thing, I think, for you, is seeing what traits of you and Babs your child has — it’s really bizarre,” Song, 38, told Sprouse, 34. “Kids pick up whatever you say. My son now goes, ‘How dare you?’ ‘cause I say that a lot.”

READ MORE: Brenda Song sends love to Macaulay Culkin as he calls his 46th birthday 'tricky'

The Wendy Wu star added, “It is so crazy to see your kids sound like you, walk like you, look like you, it’s really jarring.”

“I’m excited about that part,” Sprouse said. “That sounds fun to me,”

“It’s so much fun!” Song agreed. “Here’s the thing: I always say parenting is the hardest, most exhausting, most draining thing that I’ll ever do. But it’s also the most fulfilling, the most exciting, the most important thing I’ll ever do. As hard as it feels like in the moment, ‘cause the days will feel long, but the time feels short.”

Sprouse welcomed his first child with Palvin on September 7, a baby girl named Sylvie. The couple tied the knot in July 2023 after five years of dating.

headline: Halle Berry's Ex Olivier Martinez asks for more child support
subheadline: Judge keeps Halle Berry’s reduced visitation in place until 17 december
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Olivier Martinez has asked a court to increase the child support he receives from his ex-wife Halle Berry, saying her time with their son has fallen to about 18 per cent.

The 60-year-old actor filed court documents seeking more support from Berry, also 60.

Under the current order, set when the couple’s divorce was finalised in August 2023, she pays about $8,000 a month, plus 4.3 per cent of any income above $2 million.

Read more: Halle Berry reacts as Olivier Martinez retains primary custody of their son

Martinez’s filing says that arrangement “reflects the parties’ 50-50 physical custody of the minor child,” but argues her parenting time has “decreased to approximately 18%.”

He asks for “fair, timely, and sufficient support” that reflects California’s cost of living, and wants updated income disclosures. The amount he is requesting has not been reported.

The filing follows a custody fight that began on 1 October, when Martinez filed for sole custody of their son.

The same day, a judge temporarily changed Berry’s visitation, limiting it to Mondays, Tuesdays, Saturdays and Sundays from 10am to 8pm.

The judge refused a request to monitor Berry’s sobriety, citing “insufficient information.” On 9 November, a judge ruled the modified schedule will stay in place until 17 December.

A week before the support filing, Martinez asked Berry to pay $240,000 in legal fees, saying he lacks the resources for the mounting costs.

His October filing alleged that Berry physically abused their son during a 26 September incident.

These claims are unproven.

Martinez told PEOPLE his “paramount concern is and always has been the health, welfare, and safety of our son.”

Berry denies the claims.

In a declaration filed on 5 October, she wrote: “I have never physically, emotionally, or otherwise abused Maceo.” She says she is a victim of domestic violence.

Martinez’s temporary restraining order was dissolved, and his request for a domestic violence restraining order was denied in October.

Read more: Halle Balle's daughter says mom is 'strict when necessary' but not abusive

headline: Instagram to use AI to guess users' age, restrict accounts even if they claim to be adults
subheadline: Teenagers will not be banned simply for being under 18
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Instagram will now use artificial intelligence to estimate users' ages and automatically restrict their accounts if it suspects they are teenagers, even if they signed up using a fake date of birth.

Meta, the parent company of Instagram and Facebook, announced the global expansion on Monday, saying the technology would help identify millions of teenagers who have been using the platform without age-appropriate restrictions.

The system analyses signals from users' activity to determine whether they are under 18, rather than relying entirely on the birthdays entered when accounts are created.

Those identified as teenagers will automatically be placed into Instagram's Teen Accounts, which limit who can contact them, restrict potentially harmful content and provide additional parental controls.

Users aged 16 and below also require parental permission to change certain safety settings.

However, teenagers will not be banned simply for being under 18. Meta separately uses technology to identify and remove accounts belonging to children under 13.

The company said parents in the United States would begin receiving notifications this month explaining how the age-detection system works.

In Australia, Instagram is also using Apple's age-range information as an additional way to determine whether users are children.

The changes come after Meta agreed to multibillion-dollar settlements in lawsuits accusing its social media platforms of harming young people's mental health.

Meta has denied allegations of deliberately harming children but agreed to strengthen its safety measures.

The technology is also being introduced on Facebook, with a similar rollout planned for Threads later this year.

Meta has urged other social media platforms, including TikTok and YouTube, to adopt comparable measures.

headline: GTA VI will stream to Xbox One on day one via Xbox Cloud gaming
subheadline: Rockstar confirms GTA VI cloud streaming for Xbox One and Series X|S at launch
author: Web Desk
article_text:
It was confirmed by Rockstar Games that Grand Theft Auto VI is going to be playable on Xbox One consoles using Xbox Cloud Gaming from the day of its launch, which falls on November 19, 2026.

This implies that owners of the console released back in 2013 have access to this highly anticipated game without having to purchase a next-gen console.

According to Microsoft, the version of the game that will be streamed in the cloud will feature Xbox Series S graphics and will be available on Xbox One and Xbox Series X|S starting from 1am ET launch day. The game needs to be purchased individually, and it can also be played in the cloud without a Game Pass subscription starting on November 11.

However, the cloud offer seems limited to Xbox consoles. Although Xbox Cloud Gaming normally supports gaming on PCs, smartphones, and smart TVs, Rockstar Games confirmed that the stream for GTA VI will not be available on PCs, most likely to protect its PC release later. Microsoft calls this move "the first step in our new 10-year strategic partnership with Take-Two."

In yet another confirmation, Rockstar made it clear that GTA VI will have a constant frame rate of 30 fps on all the consoles, whether PS5, PS5 Pro, or Xbox Series X|S. This decision was informed by hardware limitations, as the game was developed “from the ground up” and designed to exploit current-generation consoles to their “absolute limits.” Those with a PS5 Pro will benefit from enhanced visuals through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution and ray-traced shadows.

The 30fps cap has sparked some debate among gamers, especially with input lag when streaming to less powerful hardware. Some gamers observed that even though the Xbox One players could technically “play” the game, it is done through servers, meaning it is not played on the console itself.

GTA VI is currently the most pre-ordered game ever in both PlayStation and Xbox stores. A PC version of the game is said to be planned for early 2027, although there is no confirmation from Rockstar yet.

headline: Sade will not attend Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction: 'Sorry'
subheadline: Sade apologises to fans for Rock Hall no-show
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Sade will not attend this year’s Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony in person, joining Oasis as another act to skip the event.

The English band, made up of reclusive lead singer Sade Adu, Paul Denman, Stuart Matthewman and Andrew Hale, announced on Tuesday that they will not appear at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, where the ceremony takes place on Saturday.

“Sorry we can’t be there in person to celebrate with the other artists,” the group said in a statement obtained by Page Six.

“Please know that our absence takes nothing away from how much this recognition means to us.”

They described the induction as “both a gift and a timely reminder to give thanks, not only to those who voted for us, but also every single person who lets our music into their lives… we are indebted to the ones who’ve been with us on this road to get here.”

The Kiss of Life band thanked their longtime manager, Roger Davis, and ended their message by honouring their “fifth Sade”, Mike Pela, a longtime collaborator who died after a sudden illness in 2022.

“This is as much yours as ours Mike forever our soul mate,” they wrote.

Sade are being inducted in the Performer category alongside Phil Collins, Billy Idol, Iron Maiden, Oasis, Joy Division/New Order, Luther Vandross and Wu-Tang Clan.

Rolling Stone reported on Monday that Oasis will not attend.

Liam Gallagher responded to a disappointed fan on X, writing: “It’s too far to be going for the night I got sh-t to do it’s Christmas.”

Unlike Gallagher, Sade gave no reason for their absence.

headline: Florence Pugh sets clear boundaries for film sets
subheadline: Florence Pugh says she will not tolerate rudeness to crews
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Florence Pugh has said she no longer tolerates bad behaviour on film sets.

She told Elle that she has learned how to lead a production and protect herself.

“Every time I work on a movie, I get more confident in the way that I can protect myself and the way that I can lead a film set, and just not stand for bullshit anymore. I’m not doing it,” Pugh said.

Read more: Florence Pugh mourns her 'The Wonder' director Sebastián Lelio

“I’m not standing for bullshit behaviour. I’m not standing for bullshit attitude. I’m not allowing for people to be rude to the crew.”

She said confidence comes with experience, and that she now wants to work with the right people. Once someone makes the atmosphere feel off, she said, “everybody feels it.”

The Oscar nominee was clear about what she wants from colleagues.

“I don’t want to deal with messy,” she said. “It’s just about surrounding yourself with professionals who have the same way of working in mind: Show up on time, don’t be rude, don’t be a misogynist.”

Pugh is enjoying a strong end to the year.

Her performance in Netflix’s East of Eden has drawn acclaim, and she will be in two big releases on 18 December: Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three.

Read more: Florence Pugh breaks her privacy rule with Finn Cole romance

headline: Ships remain ablaze, oil supplies under threat as war turns Hormuz into maritime war zone
subheadline: 37 ships attacked in October, the highest monthly total since the war began, Washington Institute data shows
author: Reuters
article_text:
US forces disable St Kitts-flagged vessel after visit to Iranian port.
Three tankers targeted over "unauthorised routes" through Hormuz.
Oil spills reach Omani shores, satellite imagery shows pollution off Oman, UAE.

Market hopes of an Iran war de-escalation are colliding with a fresh wave of attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and energy infrastructure across the Middle East.

Crude prices hit two-month lows on Tuesday after US officials played down the need for further military action against Iran, with analysts pointing to President Donald Trump's more conciliatory tone since Republicans' defeat in the November 3 midterm elections.

But there has been little sign of attacks abating this month. A total of 37 ships were attacked in October, the highest monthly figure since the start of the war, according to data from the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.

Videos posted on social media on Sunday and verified by Reuters showed the Navig8 Messi, a Singapore-flagged medium-sized refined products tanker, on fire off the coast of Oman. An image captured by the European Union's Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite on the same day showed a large plume of black smoke rising from the area.

The vessel was among three tankers hit on Sunday for using "unauthorised routes" through the strait, Iranian state broadcaster IRIB reported, citing the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy.

Navig8, which manages the vessel and is majority-owned by ADNOC Logistics & Services, did not respond to Reuters requests for comment. ADNOC also did not reply.

Meanwhile, US forces continued enforcing a naval blockade of Iranian ports. In the latest incident, a US military aircraft fired on and disabled a St Kitts-flagged cargo vessel that attempted to leave regional waters after visiting an Iranian port on Saturday, US Central Command said.

The attacks have also raised environmental concerns, with damaged vessels leaking oil into surrounding waters. A video shared on social media on Monday and verified by Reuters showed oil reaching Oman's shoreline, while satellite imagery revealed spills off the coasts of Oman and the United Arab Emirates. The Omani government did not respond to a Reuters request for comment on the footage.

Elsewhere in the region, energy infrastructure and civilian facilities have also come under attack. Iranian forces and their regional allies have struck targets including the offices of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company.

Video verified by Reuters showed damage to an Aramco office building in Riyadh following missile strikes claimed by Yemen's Houthi movement on November 8. Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said the building had been targeted in an attempted attack, with falling debris causing limited damage. No injuries or fatalities were reported.

The maritime toll has continued to rise. The International Maritime Organisation (IMO) said it had recorded 133 confirmed incidents involving commercial vessels in the region as of November 10, with 25 seafarers killed since the conflict began. Thousands of crew members remain at risk, including those aboard ships unable to leave the Persian Gulf.

The IMO Council has called for stronger protection of seafarers and urged countries to avoid measures that could jeopardise the safety of international shipping.

In the latest reported incident, a tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile 19 nautical miles northeast of Oman's Lima on Tuesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said. Its crew were safe, and no environmental impact was reported.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy separately said two tankers had caught fire after striking naval mines while using what it described as an "unauthorised route" through the strait.

  • Three tankers targeted over "unauthorised routes" through Hormuz.
  • Oil spills reach Omani shores, satellite imagery shows pollution off Oman,  UAE.

Market hopes of an Iran war de-escalation are colliding with a fresh wave of attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and energy infrastructure across the Middle East.

Crude prices hit two-month lows on Tuesday after US officials played down the need for further military action against Iran, with analysts pointing to President Donald Trump's more conciliatory tone since Republicans' defeat in the November 3 midterm elections.

But there has been little sign of attacks abating this month. A total of 37 ships were attacked in October, the highest monthly figure since the start of the war, according to data from the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.

Videos posted on social media on Sunday and verified by Reuters showed the Navig8 Messi, a Singapore-flagged medium-sized refined products tanker, on fire off the coast of Oman. An image captured by the European Union's Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite on the same day showed a large plume of black smoke rising from the area.

The vessel was among three tankers hit on Sunday for using "unauthorised routes" through the strait, Iranian state broadcaster IRIB reported, citing the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy.

Navig8, which manages the vessel and is majority-owned by ADNOC Logistics & Services, did not respond to Reuters requests for comment. ADNOC also did not reply.

Meanwhile, US forces continued enforcing a naval blockade of Iranian ports. In the latest incident, a US military aircraft fired on and disabled a St Kitts-flagged cargo vessel that attempted to leave regional waters after visiting an Iranian port on Saturday, US Central Command said.

The attacks have also raised environmental concerns, with damaged vessels leaking oil into surrounding waters. A video shared on social media on Monday and verified by Reuters showed oil reaching Oman's shoreline, while satellite imagery revealed spills off the coasts of Oman and the United Arab Emirates. The Omani government did not respond to a Reuters request for comment on the footage.

Elsewhere in the region, energy infrastructure and civilian facilities have also come under attack. Iranian forces and their regional allies have struck targets including the offices of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company.

Video verified by Reuters showed damage to an Aramco office building in Riyadh following missile strikes claimed by Yemen's Houthi movement on November 8. Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said the building had been targeted in an attempted attack, with falling debris causing limited damage. No injuries or fatalities were reported.

The maritime toll has continued to rise. The International Maritime Organisation (IMO) said it had recorded 133 confirmed incidents involving commercial vessels in the region as of November 10, with 25 seafarers killed since the conflict began. Thousands of crew members remain at risk, including those aboard ships unable to leave the Persian Gulf.

The IMO Council has called for stronger protection of seafarers and urged countries to avoid measures that could jeopardise the safety of international shipping.

In the latest reported incident, a tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile 19 nautical miles northeast of Oman's Lima on Tuesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said. Its crew were safe, and no environmental impact was reported.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy separately said two tankers had caught fire after striking naval mines while using what it described as an "unauthorised route" through the strait.

At least 22 civilian vessels, including tankers, container ships and bulk carriers, have been attacked over the past two weeks. — Reuters

headline: Jenna Bush Hager on how she handled son's questions about love life
subheadline: Jenna Bush Hager keeps dating history 'higher-level' with seven-year-old son
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Jenna Bush Hager has revealed how she handled a series of questions from her seven-year-old son, Hal, about the boys she liked before she met her husband.

The Today co-host, 44, told the story on Today with Jenna & Shenielle on Tuesday 10 November, with Willie Geist guest co-hosting.

She said she and Hal watched a romantic comedy at the weekend while her husband, Henry Hager, was away.

Read more: Jenna Bush Hager on how she handled son's questions about love life

Afterwards, Hal asked whether she had ever liked anyone the way the girl in the film liked her love interest. She said yes, his father: “Yes, your father.”

He then wanted to know if she had liked other guys before his dad. Bush Hager said she “had to go through the old roster,” although she kept the details “higher-level” and left out the “entry levels.”

Partway through the conversation, she said she began to wonder why she was sharing all of this, asking herself what she was doing.

When Hal asked why she liked those earlier boyfriends, she had to admit she could not remember, since it was about 25 years ago. She went along with it, she said, because she wanted him to learn about the joys of dating.

Bush Hager and Henry Hager have three children, two daughters and Hal.

Read more: Jenna Bush Hager embarks on new career path

headline: Hegseth survives impeachment threat as Republicans block congressional vote
subheadline: Trump hails development, says impeachment bid "miserably FAILED", calls Hegseth "Great American Patriot"
author: Reuters
article_text:
Hegseth defended his record at rare Pentagon briefing.
Trump backs Hegseth as defence chief attacks his critics.
Vote buys him time before Democrats take control of House.

Republicans in the US House of Representatives blocked an effort on Tuesday to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, winning a reprieve for the polarising Pentagon chief before Democrats take control of Congress next year and possibly try again.

The vote on a procedural motion came just hours after Hegseth blasted efforts to impeach him as a farce and delivered a defiant defence of his record at the helm of the US military, winning praise from President Donald Trump.

The chamber voted 211 to 204 in favour of a motion to refer eight articles of impeachment to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee, a move that the sponsor of the impeachment push, US Representative Thomas Massie, warned would kill it.

Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, had hoped to draw votes from Republicans upset with Hegseth's policies and wary of the unpopularity of the Iran war, but no other Republicans joined him. Democrats had voiced strong support for the impeachment effort, but 11 failed to show up to vote.

Trump cheered the vote in a social media post, saying the effort to impeach Hegseth "has miserably FAILED!"

In a sign that the impeachment episode may have drawn Trump and Hegseth closer together, Trump added that Hegseth's performance on Iran, Venezuela and other issues "led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot."

Hegseth would have been the first US defence secretary to be impeached. The last time any civilian leader of the US military was impeached was in 1876, when William Belknap held the title "secretary of war."

Hegseth calls himself secretary of war, part of his effort to rebrand a military he said was too weak and "woke" when he took office last year. Trump cannot change the name of the Department of Defence without approval from Congress.

Iran war anger

Voter anger over the Iran war, which has settled into an effective stalemate focused on securing the Strait of Hormuz, helped Democrats win control of Congress in last week's midterm elections.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries took aim at Hegseth ahead of the vote, saying on Monday: "Pete Hegseth has abused his power, undermined America's national security, and he's the architect of the reckless and costly failed war of choice in Iran."

But Hegseth repeatedly defended the conflict, calling Trump courageous and saying Iran's military has been left in ruins. He also said his orders to US forces were lawful, despite Massie's accusations of "high crimes and misdemeanours" ranging from the war itself to the US military raid in January to depose Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.

"History will judge the Iran war quite differently than the conventional wisdom right now," he said.

Massie said he was disappointed by the vote, comparing Republicans to passengers content to go down with the Titanic.

"They know it's a sinking ship but committed to stay on board," he said.

Voter anger over the Iran war, which has settled into an effective stalemate focused on securing the Strait of Hormuz, helped Democrats win control of Congress in last week's midterm elections.

"History will judge the Iran war quite differently than the conventional wisdom right now," he said.

headline: Kensington Palace reveals Prince William's favourite Lionesses moment
subheadline: Sarina Wiegman beams beside Prince William after receiving her honorary Damehood
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Prince William shared a warm moment with Sarina Wiegman at Windsor Castle as the Lionesses boss received one of the biggest honours of her career.

Wiegman was presented with an honorary Damehood by the Prince of Wales in recognition of her outstanding contribution to football on Tuesday.

Reflecting on the occasion, Wiegman said she felt “very privileged” to receive the honour from William and admitted it was a day she would never forget.

The England manager also thanked the British public for the respect and warmth she has received throughout her time with the Lionesses, as well as everyone who has supported her along the way.

Her recognition follows a remarkable spell in charge of England’s women’s team, including back-to-back European Championship triumphs.

Kensington Palace shared a photograph of the future king alongside the delighted Wiegman on Instagram, congratulating her for her contribution to women’s football and praising her success with the Lionesses.

“Thank you for everything you’ve done for women’s football, and the back-to-back Euros with the Lionesses!” the Palace wrote.

The Wales Instagram account also posted a video inside the Windsor ceremony, sharing moments of William greeting and shaking hands with the recipients who gathered to receive their honours.

headline: Prince Harry hailed as ‘true champion' amid Thomas Markle's second arrest
subheadline: Meghan Markle’s father Thomas back in custody after breaking ankle monitor
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Meghan Markle’s father, Thomas Markle, has been arrested for a second time in just four days after allegedly cutting off his court-ordered ankle monitor in Florida.

Thomas Sr. was taken into custody shortly after the monitoring device was allegedly removed, according to First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli, who confirmed the arrest in a post on X.

A Department of Justice spokesperson told PEOPLE that Meghan’s father had been due to appear in court on Tuesday, November 10, at 2.30pm EST.

Read More: Is Meghan Markle's future really at stake because of her father?

However, he allegedly removed his ankle monitor at 1.45am that same day.

Following the incident, US Magistrate Judge Lindsay S. Griffin revoked his pretrial release.

In her order, she cited concerns that Thomas had been “tampering with and removing device”.

The latest development comes as Prince Harry has been making headlines in London for his work promoting sustainable tourism.

Prince Harry has received praise for his commitment to sustainable travel after meeting the head of the World Travel & Tourism Council (WTTC) at the Wanderlust Reader Travel Awards in London.

WTTC President and CEO Gloria Guevara shared a photograph with the Duke of Sussex, describing him as a “true champion of sustainable tourism” and welcoming his message about making travel more responsible.

Guevara highlighted Harry’s comments on supporting local communities and finding ways to improve the future of tourism.

Read More: Meghan Markle reacts to reporters asking about father's arrest

The Duke founded Travalyst to bring together organisations across the industry and encourage more sustainable practices.

headline: Brenda Song makes shocking claims about Disney's 'Suite Life' shows
subheadline: Brenda Song says cast felt 'underpaid' on Disney’s 'Suite Life' shows
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Brenda Song has said she and her Suite Life castmates were “underpaid and overworked” during their years at Disney Channel, and recalled passing out on set after a hot tub malfunctioned.

The actress spoke on Wildmen, the podcast hosted by her former co-star Dylan Sprouse and Brendan Columbus.

“I think the only thing that was hard about that time was I feel like we were underpaid and overworked,” she said.

Read more: Kate Hudson, Brenda Song kids may be headed for Hollywood

Song, who played London Tipton, stressed that she had a “lovely time” on The Suite Life of Zack and Cody, which ran from 2005 to 2008, and its follow-up The Suite Life on Deck, which ran from 2008 to 2011.

She also described the moment she collapsed during a scene in a hot tub.

Sprouse said the tub had mistakenly been set to 250 degrees, twice the temperature that US health authorities regard as safe.

“I just remember breathing heavy and my chest felt really hot. I just went, ‘Am I having a panic attack?’” Song said, before she lost consciousness.

Sprouse said everyone else on set had complained about the conditions, but not Song.

“If you didn’t pass out, you wouldn’t have said anything,” he told her. He said the crew reacted with alarm after she collapsed. Neither could remember which episode it was.

Money was another sore point.

Song joked that “we paid them” when it came to residuals. Sprouse said he received a single residual cheque for five cents, from a Hannah Montana crossover.

Phill Lewis, who played Mr Moseby, has alleged that cast members were not paid for “wraparound” footage shot for future episodes. Sprouse and Lewis estimated that around 190 episodes were shot.

Since leaving Disney Channel, Song has appeared in The Last Showgirl, The Social Network, Running Point, Dollface and Dads.

headline: Johnny Depp's 'Ebenezer' salary revealed
subheadline: Johnny Depp’s first major Hollywood role since 2018 opens 13 November
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Johnny Depp took a $5 million salary for his Hollywood comeback in Ebenezer.

According to Variety, this is a fraction of what he has earned on previous studio films. The actor’s fee also includes bonuses linked to the film’s box-office performance.

Read more: Johnny Depp makes emotional confession after return to Hollywood

Ebenezer, a new take on A Christmas Carol directed by Ti West of the X horror trilogy, opens in cinemas on Friday 13 November. It is Depp’s first major Hollywood role since Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald in 2018.

Depp plays a curmudgeonly businessman who is visited by the ghosts of Christmas past, present and future. In the trailer, he scares villagers and stays stingy with Christmas bonuses.

Paramount reportedly spent about $38 million making the film and around $50 million on marketing, though it declined to comment on the figures.

Tracking suggests an opening of about $20 million in the US and Canada, with another $20 million from 63 overseas markets.

Cinema owners are cautiously hopeful.

Mark O’Meara, who runs theatres in Fairfax, Virginia, said reactions have been mixed rather than divided.

Regal chief executive Eduardo Acuna said he is optimistic, arguing the part suits Depp and the filmmaker has his own style.

Classic Cinemas chief executive Chris Johnson said the film will succeed or fail on whether it is compelling, and that audiences seem forgiving.

Audience research points the same way.

An April 2026 study by the National Research Group ranked Depp among the top ten actors who would most interest people in seeing a film in theatres.

Researcher Kevin Goetz said audiences do not care about the controversy surrounding him.

Since leaving the studio films, Depp has appeared in Minamata in 2020 and Jeanne du Barry in 2023, and directed Modì, Three Days on the Wing of Madness in 2024.

He also has a reported $20 million deal with Dior. The result may also shape his future.

Depp has said he is open to playing Jack Sparrow again, mainly to give Pirates of the Caribbean a better ending, and sources say Disney is weighing the reaction to Ebenezer before it approves another film.

Read more: Johnny Depp sets one major condition for his return as Jack Sparrow

headline: Taylor Swift, Travis Kelce win landscaping fight against Ohio neighbours
subheadline: Taylor Swift And Travis Kelce’s Ohio neighbours lose fight
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce have won approval for the landscaping plans at their $5.35 million lakefront home in Bratenahl, Ohio, despite objections from some of their neighbours.

The village’s Architectural Review Board met at the Bratenahl Community Center on Tuesday and unanimously approved the couple’s revised plans, Page Six reports.

Those plans include 10-foot shrubs, planted for privacy, and updated brickwork. Around 35 people attended, and several residents raised concerns about the shrubs.

Read more: Taylor Swift, Travis Kelce's mood leaves fans questioning their exit

Lucy Weller was worried about wildlife.

She said the couple’s team should “go back and learn a bit about native species and designs that show what animals need in this area,” arguing that the landscaping does nothing to provide for local animals.

Chuck Bauernschmidt, who said he lives two houses down, said he felt “bad for the village.” He told the board: “This is a forest, and I’m not sure why the board is going in that direction.”

Swift and Kelce did not attend.

They were represented by property manager Patrick Hyland, architect Derek Kuryla and project manager Jacob Kutz.

The couple also had supporters in the room.

Vasiliki Diamantis drew applause when she said: “We should feel privileged that these people chose this location for their residence and instead we are arguing over landscape and privacy.”

She added: “We should accept them regardless of how many days they live here.”

Another resident agreed, saying it would be “an absolute sin” if the community did anything other than welcome the pair “with open arms.”

One attendee called the discussion “stupid”, claiming the property would be “sold in seven to 10 years when the divorce happens.” The remark was booed.

The couple had already secured approval in September for a six-foot privacy fence, which also met with local concerns.

Swift and the Kansas City Chiefs tight end, who married in July, bought the eight-bedroom, 11-bathroom mansion in March.

Page Six reports that they will not use it as their main residence. Swift also owns homes in Rhode Island, Beverly Hills, Nashville and New York City.

Read more: Taylor Swift, Karlie Kloss leave fans stunned with unexpected reunion

headline: Kevin Bacon's son Travis on being 'nepo baby': 'I think it's funny'
subheadline: Travis Bacon says audiences see the 'highlight reels' but not the rejection
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Travis Bacon, the son of Kevin Bacon and Kyra Sedgwick, has said he now embraces being called a “nepo baby” and finds the label funny.

The 37-year-old musician spoke on the podcast Nepo, Baby!, hosted by Jake Robards and Emily Wachtel, in an episode recorded on 5 November.

“I think at this point I just sort of embrace the term and I think it’s funny,” he said.

Read more: Kevin Bacon's son Travis on being 'nepo baby': 'I think it's funny'

He suggested the debate has become less meaningful over time. “It doesn’t even matter whether you’re a Nepo Baby or not a Nepo baby,” he said.

Bacon also made the point that the public only sees one side of life for the children of famous parents.

Audiences get the “highlight reels”, he said, and miss the rejection and pressure that come with it. He added: “We don’t get to choose our parents.”

Bacon has built his own career in music. He is known for his work with the industrial metal band Contracult, and also works as a film composer.

His younger sister, actress Sosie Bacon, 34, has made peace with the term as well.

Known for Smile, Smile 2, Scream and HBO’s Mare of Easttown, she has said the label no longer bothers her. “It doesn’t define how I feel about what I’ve accomplished anymore,” she said.

Their parents, Kevin Bacon, 68, and Kyra Sedgwick, 61, have been married since 1988 and are among Hollywood’s longest-standing couples.

article_html:
Travis Bacon, the son of Kevin Bacon and Kyra Sedgwick, has said he now embraces being called a “nepo baby” and finds the label funny.

The 37-year-old musician spoke on the podcast Nepo, Baby!, hosted by Jake Robards and Emily Wachtel, in an episode recorded on 5 November.

“I think at this point I just sort of embrace the term and I think it’s funny,” he said.

Read more: Kevin Bacon's son Travis on being 'nepo baby': 'I think it's funny'

He suggested the debate has become less meaningful over time. “It doesn’t even matter whether you’re a Nepo Baby or not a Nepo baby,” he said.

Bacon also made the point that the public only sees one side of life for the children of famous parents. 

Audiences get the “highlight reels”, he said, and miss the rejection and pressure that come with it. He added: “We don’t get to choose our parents.”

Bacon has built his own career in music. He is known for his work with the industrial metal band Contracult, and also works as a film composer.

His younger sister, actress Sosie Bacon, 34, has made peace with the term as well. 

Known for Smile, Smile 2, Scream and HBO’s Mare of Easttown, she has said the label no longer bothers her. “It doesn’t define how I feel about what I’ve accomplished anymore,” she said.

Their parents, Kevin Bacon, 68, and Kyra Sedgwick, 61, have been married since 1988 and are among Hollywood’s longest-standing couples.

Read more: Kevin Bacon admits that filming 'The Bondsman' disrupts his sleep

headline: The Iran toll on Trump
subheadline: Democratic control gives Congress greater capacity to probe Trump admin, hold hearings and shape legislation
author: Nasim Zehra
article_text:
The Democratic Party’s victory in the November 2026 US Congressional elections is a huge political setback for President Donald Trump. His America abroad policies have become costly at home, with Washington set to have a divided government from January onward: a president with substantial authority over diplomacy and military operations, facing a Congress controlled by his opponents.

The result does not itself rewrite US policy in West Asia, but it does change the political conditions in which that policy will be debated, funded and defended. The compelling significance lies in the convergence of two forces that Washington had often kept apart: the human consequences of US policy in the region and its material costs for Americans. The US-Israeli February aggression against Iran soon drove up fuel costs. Gaza, meanwhile, had already made the consequences of US support for Israel impossible to treat as a distant or abstract issue.

Polling before the election found that voters regarded the Iran war and the Israeli-Palestinian situation as important, alongside the economy and gas prices. Hence, the kitchen-table price tag made foreign policy harder to keep out of domestic politics. The outcome proves that Israeli criticism, unlike in the past, can no longer be assumed to carry an electoral penalty for candidates. In fact, candidates who challenged US military support for Israel and spoke up for Palestinian rights won significant victories. That marks a change from a political context in which politicians could be censured or removed from influential roles for doing this. The voter was also accepting of the distinction between Jewish people and the Zionist Israeli state’s policies laid down by several candidates.

What then are likely post-election consequences for the US’s West Asia policy? The following eight are noteworthy: one, congressional scrutiny will rise; presidential control remains. Democratic control gives Congress greater capacity to investigate the administration, hold hearings, shape legislation and contest spending. It creates pressure points around arms transfers, military operations, sanctions and humanitarian assistance. But Congress’s change of hands does not transfer complete control of foreign policy from the president. As commander-in-chief and president, Trump retains considerable authority over military and diplomatic decisions. In the immediate context, there will be more friction and oversight, not policy reversal. Republicans who have been mutely opposing the war may now be more vocal, especially those focused on the next elections, like VP Vance.

Two, unconditional support for Israel faces a more contested future. For decades, broad congressional backing for Israel will now be more openly contested, particularly by Democrats and younger voters. Pre-election polls showed declining public sympathy for Israeli policy, including military aid. The post-January Congress will question arms transfers, diplomatic protection and financial assistance on legal, political and moral fronts. Trump’s Israel policy will face greater challenge.

Three, Gaza remains a test of US credibility. The political consequences of Gaza will endure beyond any ceasefire or temporary reduction in fighting. Washington’s role in providing Israel with weapons and diplomatic cover has shaped how regional publics judge US claims to defend international law and civilian protection. A Congress willing to question those policies could press for clearer conditions on military assistance, stronger oversight of weapons use and more consistent humanitarian access. Whether those pressures become law is uncertain. But the debate will influence how Arab governments assess the domestic risks of being seen as aligned with Washington.

Four, the Iran war has become a strategic and domestic liability. The war has confronted Washington with a widening gap between military action and its benefits at home. US voters clearly see the Administration’s failure to achieve stated war objectives. Most have concluded the war was not worth its cost. While these perceptions have not prompted policy change, the war is posing increasing political, military and financial difficulties for the US, making it one of the most unpopular in US history.

Five, diplomacy may gain urgency, but not necessarily coherence. The election raises the domestic cost of a prolonged conflict, strengthening the case for an off-ramp. It does not guarantee that Washington will adopt one immediately. The president may pursue negotiations while Congress pushes for tougher oversight, or the two branches may disagree on sanctions, funding and the terms of any settlement. This could complicate US signalling to Tehran and to regional partners. A durable agreement would need to address more than an immediate pause in fighting: it would have to reduce the risk of renewed attacks, restore secure maritime transit and provide a credible framework for the nuclear dispute. A ceasefire that leaves these issues unresolved may only postpone another confrontation. At the same time, making an offer acceptable to Iran, which continues to expand its diplomatic reach and partnerships, is critical.

Six, the Gulf states will reassess the value and limits of US protection. The conflict has exposed Gulf governments to direct security and economic risks, including attacks on infrastructure and disruption to commercial shipping. Their responses have differed: some have pressed for de-escalation, while others have taken a more confrontational posture towards Iran or sought closer defence cooperation. A more divided Washington may intensify questions about the reliability of US security commitments and the costs of hosting US forces. Gulf governments are unlikely to simply abandon their US partnerships. They may, however, diversify arms suppliers, deepen regional security arrangements and preserve channels to Tehran.

Seven, regional partners will watch what Washington can sustain. Israel, Iran and Gulf capitals will all read the election for signs of how long US policy can endure under domestic pressure. A Congress that questions the costs of war may make threats of escalation less credible, but it may also complicate efforts to negotiate a settlement. Israel will have to recognise the weakening of the uncontested US backing it has long enjoyed; Iran will meanwhile weigh whether domestic opposition limits Washington’s willingness to continue fighting. Gulf states will look for assurances that any diplomatic arrangement protects their security and keeps maritime routes open. The decisive question is whether Washington can align its military objectives, diplomatic commitments and public justification – a question that will largely drive Congressional debates and a divergent policy pulls on Trump’s increasingly unpopular Iran war.

Eight, the regional order will remain contested. The election does not create a new West Asian order, but it has greatly diluted US credibility and confidence in West Asia. It adds greater uncertainty to the US-mentored security order, which is now badly damaged by conflict, weakened trust and competing security choices. Regional governments may hedge between Washington and other partners, while seeking greater control over their own defence and diplomacy. It does mean that US influence increasingly depends on how Washington moves out of this war, concludes it, and through what off-ramp. For its regional allies, the US’s performance has been hugely damaging. In the coming weeks and months, Congress can amplify demands for accountability, but there are no signs that Democrats have a coherent substitute strategy on offer.

It is a fluid period for most in the region. The administration and Congress may disagree over what the US should do, while regional actors continue to make decisions based on their immediate interests and risk perceptions.

Pakistan’s role should be considered within this wider diplomatic landscape, without overstating its reach. Its proximity to Iran, ties across the Gulf and channels to Washington give it a stake in de-escalation. Pakistan can support communication and practical diplomacy, but it is one participant among several; Qatar, Oman and other regional actors also have established mediation roles. Islamabad’s strongest contribution would be to encourage restraint, keep communication channels open and support arrangements that protect regional security and maritime trade. For Pakistan, the congressional result is a reminder that US policy can become more contested and less predictable.

The broader lesson for West Asia is sharper: when the costs of war reach American households and the consequences of policy are visible across the region, Washington’s freedom of action narrows. The election result will influence the US’s West Asia policy, given that Trump’s party has paid a heavy political price for it.

The writer is a foreign policy & international security expert. She tweets/posts @nasimzehra and can be reached at: [email protected]

headline: Usher, Chris Brown abruptly cancel SoFi stadium concert amid tensions
subheadline: Usher and Chris Brown cancel Los Angeles tour stop amid feud rumours
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Usher and Chris Brown fans in Los Angeles will have to make other plans after the R&B stars’ upcoming SoFi Stadium concert was reportedly canceled.

The pair were scheduled to bring their joint tour to the venue on Monday, November 16, but TMZ reports the show has been called off.

A screenshot shared by the outlet showed the event listed as “canceled” in a ticket holder’s Ticketmaster account, with fans set to receive refunds.

Read More: Usher and Chris Brown put aside three year long feud for upcoming tour

The timing has raised eyebrows, as the cancellation comes amid reports of tension between the singers following their November 5 concert in Atlanta.

That show reportedly started three hours late and was cut short because of a midnight curfew.

Sources claimed the delay sparked a backstage disagreement: Chris allegedly wanted to push the start time back so fans could enjoy the full performance, while Usher wanted the concert to begin as scheduled.

The reported clash quickly fueled speculation that the two were feuding. Chris, however, appeared to push back against the chatter on Instagram Stories, writing, “Internet [cap]. Don’t fall for it.”

There is no confirmation that the reported disagreement had anything to do with the Los Angeles cancellation.

The tour has already faced scheduling setbacks, with four October shows previously canceled for “health and well-being.”

Read More: Usher concertgoer addresses rejecting his advances in awkward onstage moment

For now, fans are left waiting for more details about the scrapped SoFi Stadium date.

headline: Prince George stuns with hidden talent as Prince William unveils proud moment
subheadline: Prince George takes after King Charles and Princess Kate in special skills
author: Web Desk
article_text:
It’s no secret that the Prince and Princess of Wales have taken some crucial steps, even if it meant breaking royal tradition, to provide their children with a normal upbringing.

Even though the children have a destined role set for them, especially for Prince George, it hasn’t stopped them to pursue talents other than their future royal duties.

Prince William guest-edited the latest edition of Country Life magazine and the proud father took an opportunity to highlight a special talent of his 13-year-old son.

READ MORE: Kensington Palace reveals Prince William's favourite Lionesses moment

An impressive drawing – a kingfisher seen perched on a branch – by Prince George was unveiled for the first time in the magazine.

The sketch made from colour pencils captured the subtle details of the exotic bird, believed to be found near the Waleses home in Windsor, Forest Lodge.

George – now a student at Eton College following in his father’s footsteps – seemed to have inherited the artistic skills of her mum Princess Kate, who has a degree in art history from the University of St. Andrews, and his grandfather King Charles.

The King is known to be a passionate watercolourist for much of his adult life. He has also expressed his love for art on several occasions and his paintings have been auctioned as well.

Even though George is the second in line to the throne but also interested in honing his skills.

headline: Christina Applegate shares possible reason of her health struggles
subheadline: Christina Applegate opens up about joint pain amid medical tests
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Christina Applegate is exploring another possible explanation for her ongoing health struggles — and this time, she’s wondering whether her breast implants could be playing a role.

The actress, 54, raised the concern during the recent episode of her MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

Applegate, who underwent a double mastectomy in 2008 after being diagnosed with breast cancer, said she believes her implants are due for replacement.

Read More: Christina Applegate faces another health battle after MS misdiagnosis

“And I swear, over the last five years or whatever, I thought, ‘What if they’re leaking and they’re like poisoning me?’ ” she said.

The possibility came back to mind after someone shared a study suggesting that symptoms associated with breast implants can resemble those of multiple sclerosis (MS).

Applegate had initially been diagnosed with MS in 2021, but doctors have since determined she was misdiagnosed. She said she intends to discuss the implant question with her medical team.

Meanwhile, everyday movement has become increasingly difficult. Applegate described severe joint pain and said she can barely move her right shoulder.

“I don’t know what’s going on in my joints, but I can’t move my right shoulder like at all now. I can’t lift my arm,” she said.

She added that even sitting up in bed can take around 10 minutes because of the pain.

Doctors are now investigating conditions that can produce symptoms similar to MS, including rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and Lyme disease.

Read More: Christina Applegate speaks out after 'misdiagnosed'

“We’re going into square one, just doing some testing and going one-by-one of the sister diseases to MS,” she previously explained on the podcast.

headline: First Test: Sri Lanka resume first innings as Pakistan look to dominate Day 3
subheadline: Tourists resume innings on 114-3 after recovering from early collapse on Day 2 of Rawalpindi Test
author: Sports Desk
article_text:
Sri Lanka resumed their first innings on 114-3, trailing Pakistan by 320 runs on the third day of the first Test at Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium on Wednesday.

Day 2 of the opening Test saw the tourists recovering from an early collapse to reach 114-3 in 27.1 overs at stumps.

The visitors had a difficult start to their innings, losing opener Pasindu Sooriyabandara for a seven-ball duck as Mohammad Abbas struck early to give Pakistan their first breakthrough.

Debutant Saqib Khan added to Sri Lanka's troubles by dismissing Dinesh Chandimal for just one off three deliveries, registering his maiden international wicket. The dismissal left the visitors reeling at 12-2 after 3.3 overs.

However, Lahiru Udara and Kamindu Mendis steadied the innings with a composed approach, gradually building a partnership to ease the pressure following the early setbacks.

The duo brought up a 50-run partnership, taking Sri Lanka past the half-century mark and providing much-needed stability to the innings.

Saqib struck again to claim his second wicket, dismissing Udara for 42 off 52 deliveries, including seven boundaries. His dismissal left Sri Lanka reeling at 65-3 after 16.5 overs.

Dhananjaya de Silva joined Kamindu Mendis at the crease, and the pair responded positively to Pakistan's bowling attack, putting together an unbeaten 50-run partnership to take the visitors past the 100-run mark.

However, play was once again halted early due to bad light, with Sri Lanka looking to build on their recovery when play resumes on day three.

Kamindu Mendis remained unbeaten on 40, while De Silva was not out on 22. The pair will resume Sri Lanka's innings on day three, looking to build on their recovery.

Earlier, Pakistan declared their first innings at 434-9 in 106.3 overs, with five batters, including three debutants, scoring half-centuries.

Resuming day two, Saud Shakeel and Ghazi Ghori added 96 runs for the sixth wicket, taking Pakistan past 300. However, Dilshan Madushanka dismissed Ghazi for 48 off 72 deliveries, including two boundaries, leaving Pakistan at 349-6 in 88.1 overs.

Arafat Minhas joined Shakeel and added 44 runs for the seventh wicket. Shakeel fell seven runs short of his century, scoring 93 off 199 deliveries, including nine boundaries, before Asitha Fernando dismissed him at 393-7 in 100.2 overs.

Minhas and Razaullah helped Pakistan cross 400, with the all-rounder registering his maiden Test half-century. Madushanka dismissed him for 52 off 72 deliveries, including nine boundaries and a six, while Lahiru Kumara removed Razaullah for 10 before Babar Azam declared.

Asitha Fernando and Dilshan Madushanka claimed three wickets each, while Kumara, Milan Rathnayake and Sonal Dinusha took one apiece.

Earlier, openers Azan Awais and debutant Tayyab Arif provided an 86-run partnership on day one. Azan scored 30 off 50 balls, while Tayyab made 57 off 51 deliveries.

Babar and debutant Mohammad Taha steadied the innings, adding 69 runs for the third wicket. Babar scored 50 off 58 balls before Madushanka dismissed him.

Taha completed his maiden Test half-century, scoring 51 off 105 deliveries before Dinusha removed him at 227-4. Salman Ali Agha contributed 16 before falling to Fernando, while Shakeel registered his 12th Test half-century to strengthen Pakistan's position.

headline: Katie Price makes desperate 'Love Island' hosting pitch amid Maya Jama exit
subheadline: Katie Price has offered herself as a potential replacement for Maya Jama as the host of ITV dating show, 'Love Island'
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Katie Price has offered herself as a potential replacement for Maya Jama as the host of ITV dating show, Love Island.

She previously told fans,'it was "time to throw myself into something new" and has since confirmed her new project with Netflix.

Jama took over as the host of the main show in 2023, when she was 28. Since then, she has also fronted Love Island Aftersun, Love Island Games and Love Island All Stars.

READ MORE: Katie Price faces awkward setback in search for new romance

Now, the Pricey has taken to social media and tagged the official Love Island account to express her interest in hosting role, writing: 'I would love to present Love Island.'

The move comes after the mother-of-five split from her ex Lee Andrews following their whirlwind marriage.

Katie married Lee in Dubai in January, just days after they first met. Their marriage, however, soon fell apart. She later said that he had made up stories about his life and money.

READ MORE: Katie Price gives evidence to court as ex-husband faces serious charges

headline: Imran taken to Pims overnight for check-up ahead of court-ordered jail meeting
subheadline: Jailed PTI founder was administered anti-VEGF injection in his eye, says Pims admin
author: Shabbir Dar
article_text:
Imran's hospital visit undertaken under tight security: jail sources.
Check-up included follow-up treatment for eyes: Pims admin.
Former premier transferred back to jail after check-up: sources.

RAWALPINDI: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) founder and former prime minister Imran Khan was taken from Adiala jail to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) in Islamabad late at night for a medical examination, hospital administration said on Wednesday.

According to an official statement issued by the Pims administration, jailed Imran was brought to the hospital from Adiala jail during the night between November 10 and 11.

The statement said that the examination included a follow-up treatment for his eyes.

On the recommendation of an eye specialist, the PTI founder was administered an anti-VEGF injection in his eye, with the procedure carried out by the ophthalmology department's team.

The hospital administration said that all of Imran's vital medical indicators were found to be within normal limits during the examination.

It further said that the former prime minister's overall physical condition was satisfactory and stable.

Sources said Imran was taken to the hospital under tight security arrangements, with similar security measures maintained during his return to prison following the examination.

The development came a day after the Islamabad High Court (IHC) directed that lawyers Latif Khosa and Salman Safdar be allowed to meet Imran and his wife, Bushra Bibi, in Adiala jail, with the attorney general saying the meetings could be arranged if they assured the court that arguments in the appeals would begin at the next hearing.

A division bench comprising IHC Chief Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfraz Dogar and Justice Muhammad Asif had issued directives while hearing appeals filed by Imran and Bushra against their convictions in the £190 million case.

An accountability court in Islamabad had sentenced the former prime minister to 14 years' imprisonment with a fine of Rs1 million, while the ex-first lady was awarded seven years' imprisonment along with a fine of Rs500,000.

During Tuesday's hearing, lawyer Khosa told the IHC that he had repeatedly sought a meeting with the former premier but had not been allowed to meet him.

Khosa requested at least an hour-long meeting with the PTI founder, after which the court directed the Islamabad advocate general to arrange his meeting with Imran and Bushra.

The former premier's counsel, Barrister Salman Safdar, also requested another meeting, saying his previous meeting with the PTI founder had provided instructions but was insufficient.

Safdar said Imran had told him that his eyesight had improved but his blood pressure remained uncontrolled, warning of a risk of brain haemorrhage.
